Efficient, evidence-based control programs must consider both rodent and pathogen ecology, to achieve both rodent population and pathogen transmission risk reduction. The present study aims to determine the ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus positivity in an urban Norway Rat population. One hundred and twenty rats were trapped in four urban poor communities in Salvador, Brazil, tested for Leptospira sp. and Hantavirus. Generalized Linear Models for Leptospira (N=109) and Hantavirus (N=108) positivity were created with a pool of environmental and demographic variables, followed by stepwise model selection using Akaike’s Information Criterion. Age, presence of Calodium hepaticum scars, wounds, accumulated materials, open sewer canals and unpaved soil were positively associated with Leptospira positivity. Age and presence of accumulated materials were positively associated with Hantavirus positivity, while rodent control campaigns and being male were protective factors. Factors associated with positivity for Leptospira are also associated with rodent infestation. Different subsets of environmental and demographic factors influence pathogens with different epidemiological characteristics. Control measures that effectively reduce zoonotic risk must consider the ecological characteristics of the pathogens present in the system. Similar content being viewed by others Introduction Old world rats (genus Rattus) are the most ubiquitous synanthropic animals. Their global distribution and occurrence arise from their intimate relationship with human presence, following major human movements throughout the globe, such as the Transatlantic navigation and the Silk Route (Morand et al. 2015). Currently, rats are almost exclusively associated with human occupation, often of urbanized areas, are significantly dependent on the resources made available by human activity (Feng and Himsworth 2013). The relationship between rats and humans is not harmonious, with rats being considered pests, causing damage to farming and infrastructure, and contaminating food stocks (Jacob and Buckle 2018). Estimations suggest, conservatively, that the Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus, alone causes economic damage of more than USD 30 million/year globally (Diagne et al. 2023). Throughout the Global South, the fast growth of urban centers often results in the creation of informal settlements, characterized by deficiencies in the provision and coverage of basic urban services (e.g., trash collection, sanitation, pest control) and infrastructure (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2024; Costa et al. 2014; de Oliveira et al. 2024). The resulting environment is highly conductive to rodent infestation, with an abundance of water, food and shelter (Panti-May et al. 2016). Such close coexistence exposes the populations of the settlements to the pathogens carried by rats (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Muschetto et al. 2025). The role of rats as a zoonotic pathogen reservoir is arguably one of the most impactful threats posed by our proximity. Rodents host a remarkable diversity of zoonotic pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, unicellular eukaryote and helminth parasites (Luis et al. 2013; Himsworth et al. 2013; Delaney, Treuting, and Rothenburger 2018). Some of the most historically relevant pathogens have rodents as their reservoir, such as Yersinia pestis (Rahelinirina et al. 2021), Leptospira sp. (A. Minter et al. 2017) and Hantavirus (Dearing and Dizney 2010). Depending on the pathogen, rodents can either be direct sources of infection or act as part of the transmission cycle, shedding bacteria to the environment or promoting infective contact with competent hosts that thus infect humans (Himsworth et al. 2013). Important examples of pathogens carried by Norway rats are Leptospira spp. (Feng and Himsworth 2013), Hantavirus (Chen et al. 2023), and Toxoplasma gondii (Bazan et al. 2025). Leptospira spp., the causative agent of leptospirosis, is a genus of bacteria transmitted by water and soil contaminated by the urine of infected hosts such as rats, which are asymptomatic carriers and chronic shedders of the bacteria (Guerra 2009; Tucunduva de Faria et al. 2007). With over one million estimated human cases per year (Costa et al. 2015), the infection can cause asymptomatic/mild forms or evolve into severe and potentially lethal forms such as Weil’s disease and Leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome (Ko, Goarant, and Picardeau 2009). In Salvador, leptospirosis is a long-standing challenge to public health in impoverished urban communities (Ko et al. 1999; Ribeiro et al. 2008). Hantavirus (Hantaviridae: genus Orthohantavirus) is a genus of negative-sense RNA viruses maintained mainly by small mammals (Bradfute et al. 2024), with several species pathogenic to humans. The clade is divided in Old World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus seoulense [SEOV], Orthohantavirus hantanense [HTNV]), causative agents of Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome, and New World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus andense [ANDV], Orthohantavirus sinnombreense [SNV]), causative agents of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (Chen et al. 2023). Norway rats are the main reservoirs of Orthohantavirus seoulense, with chronic, nearly asymptomatic infection (Jonsson et al.2010; Meyer and Schmaljohn 2000). SEOV is considered to be cosmopolitan following the worldwide distribution of rats (Himsworth et al. 2013) and has been previously detected in rats in Salvador (Costa et al. 2014). Toxoplasma gondii is an apicomplexan parasite that widely infects warm-blooded animals, causing grave illness in immunocompromised individuals, as well as fetal development issues through congenital toxoplasmosis (S.G. Sanchez and Besteiro 2021). While important for the epidemiology of toxoplasmosis, infection by T. gondii in rats causes behavioral changes, but limited health effects (Ruffolo et al. 2016; Webster 1994). For the control of rat-borne zoonoses, the ecology of the zoonotic system should also be considered, as this presents its own ecological characteristics (Caio et al. 2016), an important consideration given the diversity of pathogens that rats can carry, including potential coinfections (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2018; Costa et al. 2014; L.K.F. Lee et al. 2023). Previous studies in urban informal settlements in Salvador have investigated urban rodent ecology (Panti-May et al. 2016; C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021; Eyre et al. 2020), movement (Awoniyi et al. 2021), the parasites and pathogens they carry (Costa, Porter, et al. 2014; Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2018), and the impacts of infestation on human health (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Costa et al. 2021). However, studies have focused on isolated pathogens (Souza et al. 2021; Bazan et al. 2025; Pimentel Sobrinho et al. 2020), not yet evaluating potential ecological interactions between these pathogens, such as how environmental and demographic factors might differ between them. Knowledge of pathogen ecology of Norway rats, a multi-pathogen reservoir, including prevalence and pathogen characteristics and the impacts of environmental factors on their dynamics is essential to lead to targeted control and intervention strategies. Different pathogens can present different characteristics (e.g., acquisition route, tissue tropism, requirements for transmission) even if infecting the same host species, likely resulting in different responses to control measures. Our study aims to quantify zoonotic positivity for three different pathogens (Hantavirus, Leptospira spp. and Toxoplasma gondii) in Norway rats from urban impoverished communities in the city of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, and identify whether the ecological processes that drive rat infection risk vary between pathogens. Characterizing zoonotic spillover risk in rodents and identifying environmental risk factors is fundamental for the development of rodent-borne zoonosis control programs that are resilient against the risk of pathogen (re)emergence as an unpredicted negative effect of the control program itself. Materials and Methods Ethical Statement Rodent sampling and biological sample harvesting procedures were authorized under license from the Ethics Committee for Animal Use of Fiocruz Bahia (authorization #019/2016). The study was conducted and reported following ARRIVE guidelines. Study Site The city of Salvador, Bahia (12° 55′ 28.03" S, 38° 28′ 34.9′′ W) is one of the largest urban centers in Brazil, with 692,819 km2 and over 2.5 million inhabitants, 42.7% of which living in informal settlements (henceforth communities) (IBGE 2022, 2015). Four communities were sampled: Marechal Rondon (MR), Alto do Cabrito (AC), Rio Sena (RS) e Nova Constituinte (NC), selected for their location in the same sanitary district (subdivisions of the city’s territory used for the operations of health authorities, including the Zoonosis Control Center [CCZ]), reflecting their sociodemographic similarity and environmental profile, which fit the criteria for classification as slums (inadequate housing conditions, limited or absent access to safe drinking water and sanitation), (Economic and Affairs 2019), and lack of adequate solid waste collection (including formation of open trash piles). All four communities were set on hills, with small natural waterways running at their lowermost point, which receive the communities’ household sewage. According to the CCZ, the communities have chronic issues with rodent infestation. In each community, the study area was defined as a polygon of 0.07–0.09 km2. Zoonotic Positivity for Rattus Norvegicus Rat capture data, and environmental and biological samples (kidney imprints, urine, blood and brain matter) were obtained from a previous field sampling study conducted in four communities, performed in two campaigns (40 semi-randomized trapping points with two Tomahawk-type traps, 4 trap-nights per campaign, April-June and October–November 2018) (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). During necropsy and tissue sample harvesting, the presence of Calodium hepaticum (a helminth species that parasitises the liver of mammals, frequently observed in wild Rattus) was registered during the examination of the liver. The presence of the characteristic scars in the liver cortex was considered as a positive detection for the individual (Fuehrer 2014). Positivity for Leptospira was assessed by a combination of Indirect Fluorescent Antibody (IFA) assays performed on Poli-L-Lysine-treated microscope slides with kidney imprints (D et al. 2016) and/or urine sample qPCR targeting the lipL32 gene as previously described (Costa, Wunder, et al. 2015). Hantavirus positivity was determined by Enzyme-linked Immunoassay (ELISA) tests, using orthohantavirus purified recombinant nucleoprotein as antigen (Padula et al. 2000). Detection of Toxoplasma was performed through nested-PCR tests targeting the IST1 region of T. gondii (Hurtado et al. 2001). Due to limitations in availability, PCR tests for Hantavirus (RT-PCR targeting the Hantavirus-specific RNA-dependent RNA polymerase-encoding L segment) were restricted to ELISA-positive rats. All PCR tests were negative. The physical condition of rats was measured as a weight-length ratio that took into account the effect of age (Peig and Green 2009). Age of individuals was calculated in days based in morphometric data following the von Bertalanffy equation, with parameters obtained by fitting data derived from the growth curve for male rats (Calhoun 1962; Burthe et al. 2009). Morphology data, presence of parasites and of wounds were obtained during animal processing (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). Environmental Variables A standardized descriptive questionnaire was applied to obtain the environmental data used to characterize the environment at each sampling point. The data collection occurred at the moment of trapping, being performed considering a 20-m-radius buffer around the sampling point (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). Variables describe the presence of other animals, human-made materials (refuse, construction materials, debris), soil condition and presence of water, as well as rodent control activities (both carried by the locals themselves and by the Zoonosis Control Center) in the region at the moment the traps were set. Data on opossum presence were derived from captures during the trapping period. Data on presence of animals and rodent control measures in the trapping area (i.e., household backyards) were voluntarily provided by the resident during trap setting. Variables collected are listed in Table 1. Statistical Analysis To evaluate each outcome (positivity for Leptospira, Toxoplasma, or Hantavirus), a set of variables was defined based on hypotheses that link the biological processes known to be relevant to each pathogen to the outcome (Table 1). Positivity for the other pathogens was also added as a variable to evaluate if coinfection affects the chances of positivity for each zoonotic pathogen. Collinearity was verified through the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), with variables having a VIF under 5 considered apt to compose the variable pool for each outcome. Generalized linear models (GLMs) were performed for each outcome using the VIF-verified and hypothesis-associated variables, followed by backwards stepwise model selection based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Models were considered plausible when ΔAIC < 2 compared to the model with the lowest AIC and selected based on maximum parsimony (lowest ΔAIC and number of variables). All analyses were performed using the packages Tidyverse, lme4 e MuMIn, on R Core Team, 2026 (Wickham et al. 2019; Bates et al. 2015; Barton 2022). Results Zoonotic Positivity for Rattus Norvegicus One-hundred and sixteen individuals were tested for Leptospira, with 48.3% positivity (56/116); 117 tested for Hantavirus with 31.6% positivity (37/117) and 9 samples with indeterminate status; and 120 tested for Toxoplasma, with 2.5% positivity (3/120). Due to the low positivity for Toxoplasma, only Hantavirus and Leptospira were analysed by GLM and model selection. The model for Leptospira was performed with 109 individuals (7 individuals removed due to incomplete associated data), with this subset presenting 48.6% (53/109) positivity, and 108 individuals were employed for the Hantavirus model (9 individuals removed due to incomplete data), presenting 33.3% (36/108) positivity. From the subsets with complete data, 39.6% (21/53) of the Leptospira-positive rats were also positive for Hantavirus, while 58.3% (21/36) of orthohantavirus-positive rats were also positive for Leptospira. Leptospira Positivity Model Fifty-six models were considered plausible (ΔAIC <2) after model selection. Among the plausible models, five were equally parsimonious (four variables each), containing six variables between them. These six variables were age estimated in days (present in 49/56 plausible models), presence of Calodium hepaticum scars in the liver (50/56), presence of open sewers within a 20-m-radius buffer (37/56), the presence of accumulated materials (45/56), type of ground cover (54/56), and presence of wounds (56/56) (for the full model selection table, see Appendix S1: Table S1). Age in days (OR 1.02 [1–1.04], p=0.083), presence of C. hepaticum scars in the liver (OR 2.41 [0.9–6.3], p=0.084), presence of accumulated materials (OR 3.2 [0.82–14.9], p=0.109), presence of open sewers within the 20 m buffer (OR 2.03 [0.82–5.19], p=0.13), the presence of unpaved soil (OR 2.75 [1.06–7.46], p=0.041), and the presence of wounds (OR 7.62 [1.15–153.94], p=0.075) all increased the odds of positivity (Table 2). Hantavirus positivity model Forty models were considered plausible (ΔAIC<2) according to the results of model selection (for the full model selection table, see Appendix S1: Table S2). The single most parsimonious model contained four variables, namely sex (present in 40/40 plausible models), age in days (40/40), Centre for the Control of Zoonoses (CCZ) activity (38/40) and presence of accumulated materials (40/40). According to the model, CCZ activity (OR 0.32 [0.12–0.83] p=0.022) and being a male (OR 0.25 [0.08–0.66], p=0.007) reduced the odds of positivity. In contrast, age (OR 1.05 [1.02–1.07], p<0.001) and presence of accumulated materials (OR 12.42 [2.25–113.25], p=0.01) increased the odds of positivity (Table 2). Discussion Our results support the hypothesis that different pathogens are associated with different ecological variables. Only two variables analyzed were common to both pathogens – age (in days) and the presence of accumulated materials (all non-garbage items accumulated in the environment, including but not limited to piles of construction materials, construction debris and large discarded items). Infections by Leptospira were associated with environmental factors, particularly anthropogenic modifications, relevant to the environmental component of the pathogen’s transmission, namely the presence of sewage and unpaved, pervious soil (A. Minter et al. 2017), as well as with coinfection with another parasite, the nematode Calodium hepaticum. Infections by Hantavirus were associated with rodent control carried by CCZ, considered a demographic stressor (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). The ubiquitous presence of factors associated with environmental vulnerability and absence of necessary management highlights the importance of environmental health as a pillar of the One Health framework and opportunities for evidence-based management and control (Gittleman 2024). The age of individuals increased the chances of positivity for both pathogens. Leptospira spp., the causative agent of leptospirosis, is a genus of bacteria transmitted by water and soil contaminated by the urine of infected hosts such as rats, which are asymptomatic carriers and chronic shedders of the bacteria (Guerra 2009; Tucunduva de Faria et al. 2007). With over one million estimated human cases per year (Costa et al. 2015), the infection can cause asymptomatic/mild forms or evolve into severe and potentially lethal forms such as Weil’s disease and Leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome (Ko, Goarant, and Picardeau 2009). In Salvador, leptospirosis is a long-standing challenge to public health in impoverished urban communities (Ko et al. 1999; Ribeiro et al. 2008). Hantavirus (Hantaviridae: genus Orthohantavirus) is a genus of negative-sense RNA viruses maintained mainly by small mammals (Bradfute et al. 2024), with several species pathogenic to humans. The clade is divided in Old World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus seoulense [SEOV], Orthohantavirus hantanense [HTNV]), causative agents of Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome, and New World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus andense [ANDV], Orthohantavirus sinnombreense [SNV]), causative agents of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (Chen et al. 2023). Norway rats are the main reservoirs of Orthohantavirus seoulense, with chronic, nearly asymptomatic infection (Jonsson et al.2010; Meyer and Schmaljohn 2000). SEOV is considered to be cosmopolitan following the worldwide distribution of rats (Himsworth et al. 2013) and has been previously detected in rats in Salvador (Costa et al. 2014). Toxoplasma gondii is an apicomplexan parasite that widely infects warm-blooded animals, causing grave illness in immunocompromised individuals, as well as fetal development issues through congenital toxoplasmosis (S.G. Sanchez and Besteiro 2021). While important for the epidemiology of toxoplasmosis, infection by T. gondii in rats causes behavioral changes, but limited health effects (Ruffolo et al. 2016; Webster 1994). For the control of rat-borne zoonoses, the ecology of the zoonotic system should also be considered, as this presents its own ecological characteristics (Caio et al. 2016), an important consideration given the diversity of pathogens that rats can carry, including potential coinfections (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2018; Costa et al. 2014; L.K.F. Lee et al. 2023). Previous studies in urban informal settlements in Salvador have investigated urban rodent ecology (Panti-May et al. 2016; C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021; Eyre et al. 2020), movement (Awoniyi et al. 2021), the parasites and pathogens they carry (Costa, Porter, et al. 2014; Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2018), and the impacts of infestation on human health (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Costa et al. 2021). However, studies have focused on isolated pathogens (Souza et al. 2021; Bazan et al. 2025; Pimentel Sobrinho et al. 2020), not yet evaluating potential ecological interactions between these pathogens, such as how environmental and demographic factors might differ between them. Knowledge of pathogen ecology of Norway rats, a multi-pathogen reservoir, including prevalence and pathogen characteristics and the impacts of environmental factors on their dynamics is essential to lead to targeted control and intervention strategies. Different pathogens can present different characteristics (e.g., acquisition route, tissue tropism, requirements for transmission) even if infecting the same host species, likely resulting in different responses to control measures. Our study aims to quantify zoonotic positivity for three different pathogens (Hantavirus, Leptospira spp. and Toxoplasma gondii) in Norway rats from urban impoverished communities in the city of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, and identify whether the ecological processes that drive rat infection risk vary between pathogens. analysis.background: Rodent control in urban areas is vital because rats carry zoonotic pathogens; the study aims to identify ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus in urban Norway rats.
analysis.methods: 120 rats were trapped in four poor communities in Salvador, Brazil; 109 were tested for Leptospira and 108 for Hantavirus, and generalized linear models with environmental and demographic variables were built using stepwise AIC selection.
analysis.results: Leptospira positivity correlated with age, Calodium hepaticum scars, wounds, accumulated materials, open sewer canals and unpaved soil; Hantavirus positivity correlated with age and accumulated materials, while rodent control campaigns and male sex were protective.
analysis.contribution: The findings reveal that Leptospira risk factors overlap with rodent infestation, whereas different subsets of variables drive Hantavirus, indicating control programs must account for pathogen‑specific ecological characteristics.
analysis.limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence; only abstract and partial text are available.

papers.title_zh: 城市挪威鼠群体中钩端螺旋体与 汉坦病毒 的生态驱动因素差异。

analysis_zh.background: 城市地区的鼠类控制至关重要,因为老鼠携带人畜共患病原体;本研究旨在识别城市挪威鼠中钩端螺旋体和 汉坦病毒 的生态驱动因素。
analysis_zh.methods: 在巴西萨尔瓦多的四个贫困社区捕获了120只老鼠;其中109只检测了钩端螺旋体,108只检测了 汉坦病毒,并使用逐步AIC选择构建了包含环境和人口学变量的广义线性模型。
analysis_zh.results: 钩端螺旋体阳性与年龄、Calodium hepaticum 瘢痕、创伤、堆积物、开放式下水道渠和未铺设土壤相关;汉坦病毒 阳性与年龄和堆积物相关,而鼠类控制行动和雄性则具有保护作用。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果显示,钩端螺旋体的风险因素与鼠类侵扰重叠,而不同变量子集驱动 汉坦病毒,表明控制方案必须考虑病原体特异性的生态特征。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告局限性;仅有摘要和部分文本可用。

papers.title: Hantavirus RNA Detection in Small Mammals and Spatial Association with Human Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome in the West Kazakhstan Region, 2025
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease associated with orthohantaviruses maintained in natural rodent hosts. This study assessed the detection and spatial distribution of hantavirus RNA among small mammals in the West Kazakhstan Region in 2025 and compared rodent surveillance findings with human HFRS occurrence. An observational descriptive-analytical study was conducted in August–September 2025 in four districts. A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified. Lung tissues were tested using 123 pooled testing units, while 14 specimens were tested individually during the same surveillance campaign. Thus, 137 testing units representing 343 animals were evaluated by real-time and conventional RT-PCR. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive minimum estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size. Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units, including 45 positive pooled units and two individually positive specimens, corresponding to a descriptive MIR of 13.7%. The model-based individual-level infection probability was estimated at 18.0% (95% profile-likelihood CI: 13.5–23.1%). Positive testing units were observed among Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis. At the district level, the descriptive MIR ranged from 11.6% in Burlinsky to 19.0% in Chingirlauisky. Sampling sites overlapped spatially with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, including Utvinka, Daryinsk, and Rubezhinskoye; however, spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease linked to orthohantaviruses maintained in rodent reservoirs, posing public‑health concerns.
analysis.methods: An observational descriptive‑analytical study was performed in August–September 2025 across four districts of West Kazakhstan (A3). A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified (A4). Lung tissues were examined using 123 pooled and 14 individual testing units, yielding 137 testing units evaluated by real‑time and conventional RT‑PCR (A5‑A6). Minimum infection rate (MIR) and a pooled‑testing likelihood model were applied to estimate infection prevalence (A7).
analysis.results: Hantavirus RNA was found in 47 of 137 testing units, giving a descriptive MIR of 13.7% (A8); the model‑based individual infection probability was 18.0% (95% CI 13.5–23.1%) (A9). Positive units occurred in Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis (A10). District MIR ranged from 11.6% to 19.0% (A11). Sampling sites overlapped with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, though spatial coincidence does not prove transmission (A12‑A13).
analysis.contribution: The study provides surveillance data on hantavirus prevalence in rodent hosts and highlights spatial overlap with human cases, informing risk mapping and public‑health monitoring (A12‑A13).
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is available, limiting detail on sampling design and statistical analyses; spatial overlap alone cannot establish direct transmission (A13).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a rodent‑borne zoonosis of public‑health importance. Methods: An observational descriptive‑analytical study in four West Kazakhstan districts (Aug‑Sept 2025) captured 343 mammals, tested lung tissue via pooled and individual RT‑PCR, and estimated prevalence using MIR and a likelihood model. Results: Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units (descriptive MIR 13.7%); model‑based infection probability 18.0% (95% CI 13.5–23.1%). Positive rodents included Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis, with district MIR 11.6–19.0%; rodent sites overlapped human HFRS settlements, but spatial coincidence does not prove transmission. Contribution: Provides surveillance evidence and spatial risk insight for hantavirus in Kazakhstan. Limitations: Abstract‑only data; spatial overlap does not establish causation.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 RNA 检测在小型哺乳动物中,并与人类 肾综合征出血热 的空间关联,位于哈萨克斯坦西部地区,2025年

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热 (HFRS) 是一种人畜共患疾病, 与在啮齿动物宿主中维持的 正汉坦病毒 相关,构成公共卫生关注。
analysis_zh.methods: 在2025年8–9月于哈萨克斯坦西部四个区(A3)开展了一项观察性描述-分析研究。共捕获并形态鉴定了343只小型哺乳动物(A4)。使用123个合并样本和14个单独检测单元,对肺组织进行检测,共评估了137个检测单元,采用实时和常规RT‐PCR(A5‐A6)。应用最小感染率(MIR)和合并检测似然模型估算感染流行率(A7)。
analysis_zh.results: 在137个检测单元中检测到汉坦病毒 RNA,共47个阳性,描述性MIR为13.7%(A8);基于模型的单个感染概率为18.0%(95% CI 13.5–23.1%)(A9)。阳性单元出现在乌拉尔田鼠(Apodemus uralensis)、灰田鼠(Myodes glareolus)和田原田鼠(Microtus arvalis)中(A10)。各区MIR范围为11.6%至19.0%(A11)。采样点与报告有人类肾综合征出血热病例的定居点重合,尽管空间重合并不证明传播(A12‐A13)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提供了关于汉坦病毒 在啮齿动物宿主中流行率的监测数据,并强调了与人类病例的空间重合,为风险绘图和公共卫生监测提供信息(A12‐A13)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要信息可得,限制了对采样设计和统计分析的细节描述;仅凭空间重合无法确定直接传播(A13)。

papers.title: Hantaan virus polymerase has an in vitro Terminal Nucleotidyl Transferase activity that is conserved across the Bunyaviricetes class
papers.abstract: Abstract Abstract section Bunyaviricetes is a class of segmented negative strand RNA viruses (sNSV) that includes causative agents of severe zoonotic diseases resulting in hemorrhagic fever in humans and livestock. Hantaan virus (HTNV), family Hantaviridae , is an example of life-threatening bunyavirus transmitted by rodents which leads to Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans. Infection relies on the replication and transcription of their tripartite genomes through multifunctional RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) in the context of ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) made of one viral RNA fragment, one RdRp and multiple copies of viral nucleoproteins. The RdRp, also known as L protein, performs replication by de novo initiation through a prime-and-realign mechanism while transcription initiates through a cap snatching mechanism, that engages a cap-binding domain and an endonuclease (EN) domain present in the L protein C and N terminal regions, respectively. In this work we show that HTNV L protein has a terminal nucleotidyl transferase (TNTase) activity over double-stranded RNA substrates (dsRNA) in vitro . We show that the TNTase activity is also present in other bunyaviral L proteins by comparing HTNV L protein activity with La Crosse (LACV, family Orthobunyaviridae ) and Crimean Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV, family Nairoviridae ) L proteins. Our results show that TNTase activity appears to be a general feature of Bunyaviruses and report the differences on substrate and nucleotide specificity for each family of virus. Importance The L proteins are preferential antiviral targets for the treatment of bunyaviral emerging diseases. Our results provide new ground for the characterization of L protein enzymatic activity in vitro which should be considered for the development activity assays, paramount for the screening of antiviral compounds. Indeed, TNTase activity can be easily misinterpreted as replication activity. We indicate here the key experimental setup and controls that would need to be considered to distinguish both activities. Our in vitro observations pave the way for future investivation of the potential TNTase role(s) in the infected cells. Proposed hypotheses concern potential functions in the preservation of genome integrity, the prevention of RIG-I innate immune response activation, or modification of RNA metabolism in the cell cytoplasm. The TNTase activity assays we describe here finally provide a straightforward biochemical approach for screening of inhibitors targeting RdRp activity.

source_records.abstract: Abstract Abstract section Bunyaviricetes is a class of segmented negative strand RNA viruses (sNSV) that includes causative agents of severe zoonotic diseases resulting in hemorrhagic fever in humans and livestock. Hantaan virus (HTNV), family Hantaviridae , is an example of life-threatening bunyavirus transmitted by rodents which leads to Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans. Infection relies on the replication and transcription of their tripartite genomes through multifunctional RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) in the context of ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) made of one viral RNA fragment, one RdRp and multiple copies of viral nucleoproteins. The RdRp, also known as L protein, performs replication by de novo initiation through a prime-and-realign mechanism while transcription initiates through a cap snatching mechanism, that engages a cap-binding domain and an endonuclease (EN) domain present in the L protein C and N terminal regions, respectively. In this work we show that HTNV L protein has a terminal nucleotidyl transferase (TNTase) activity over double-stranded RNA substrates (dsRNA) in vitro . We show that the TNTase activity is also present in other bunyaviral L proteins by comparing HTNV L protein activity with La Crosse (LACV, family Orthobunyaviridae ) and Crimean Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV, family Nairoviridae ) L proteins. Our results show that TNTase activity appears to be a general feature of Bunyaviruses and report the differences on substrate and nucleotide specificity for each family of virus. Importance The L proteins are preferential antiviral targets for the treatment of bunyaviral emerging diseases. Our results provide new ground for the characterization of L protein enzymatic activity in vitro which should be considered for the development activity assays, paramount for the screening of antiviral compounds. Indeed, TNTase activity can be easily misinterpreted as replication activity. We indicate here the key experimental setup and controls that would need to be considered to distinguish both activities. Our in vitro observations pave the way for future investivation of the potential TNTase role(s) in the infected cells. Proposed hypotheses concern potential functions in the preservation of genome integrity, the prevention of RIG-I innate immune response activation, or modification of RNA metabolism in the cell cytoplasm. The TNTase activity assays we describe here finally provide a straightforward biochemical approach for screening of inhibitors targeting RdRp activity.

HTNV is a 52 rodent-borne virus, a widely distributed and prototype virus of Hantavirus, whose 53 3 human infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome reaching mortality rates 54 up to 12% (2). It is thus a crucial target for the development of antivirals and prevention 55 strategies to face future pandemic threats, as the recent outbreak of the related Andes 56 hantavirus in a cruise ship in may 2026 (3-6). HTNV have a three-segmented genome 57 consisting on small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments, based on their size, which 58 encode for the nucleoprotein (N), membrane glycoproteins Gn and Gc, and viral RNA- 59 dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) (also called L protein), respectively (7, 8). 60 The L proteins are multifunctional proteins responsible for both (i) viral RNA replication 61 that initiates de novo in the absence of primer, and (ii) viral transcription that initiates 62 through a cap-snatching mechanism characteristic of sNSVs (9, 10). Cap-snatching 63 consists of holding a cellular capped RNA through the L protein cap-binding domain, 64 prior to its cleavage by the L protein endonuclease (EN) domain and the subsequent use 65 of obtained RNA capped oligonucleotide for the priming of the transcription reaction (8). 66 Transcription and replication occur in the context of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assemblies 67 where each segment is coated by multiple copies of viral nucleoproteins and one L 68 protein. Bunyaviricetes L proteins and influenza heterotrimeric polymerases specifically 69 recognize their genomes by specific interactions with their 5 and 3 vRNA genomic ends 70 which have specific binding sites in the protein surface. The vRNAs maintain a 5-3 distal 71 duplex by complementary bases that is essential for replication and transcription 72 initiation (11). The 5 binding site recognizes the 5 vRNA as a hook which is important 73 for the regulation of the polymerase activity by allosterically activating the RdRp active 74 site (10, 12). Two 3 binding sites have been shown for sNSVs polymerases (13). The 75 primary binding site is in the active site placing the 3 template ready for de novo 76 replication or cap-snatching transcription initiation. The secondary binding site for the 77 vRNA 3 end is at the surface of sNSV polymerases keeping the template’s ends attached 78 to the polymerase during transcription and replication elongation. This RNA promoter 79 binding strategy allows to keep the RNP circular throughout all the RNA synthesis 80 process (14) (15) (16). 81 Enzymatic assays coupled to structural studies have been key for unveiling such 82 sophisticated mechanism of genome processing by the RdRp of sNSV (10, 14, 17-19). 83 Some species-specific behaviors highlight variations on this general functional trend. For 84 4 instance, EN have been shown to be active or inactive in vitro and this is related to the 85 presence or absence of a catalytic histidine in the EN active site (classified as His+ and 86 His- ENs respectively) (20) (21). Is not clear how L proteins with His- ENs, such as those 87 of arenaviruses and nairoviruses, perform cap-snatching. On another hand, Arenavirus 88 L protein structure was reported together with biochemical assays showing a 89 constitutively active polymerase in absence of 5 vRNA (22) which contrasted with 90 polymerase assays reporting the need of the dsRNA promoter with a non-templated 5 91 G in the 5vRNA (18), a non-templated nucleotide naturally present in arenavirus 92 genomes. In arenaviruses the polymerase activity is regulated by the small viral protein 93 Z, which is unique to this viral family (23). Thus, further studies on replication and 94 transcription activities are required for the precise comprehension of L protein activities 95 and their regulation for each particular bunyaviral family. 96 All viruses with an RNA genome face the challenge of maintaining the genome integrity 97 which may be affected by cellular RNA modifications or high RdRp error rates. Most 98 Bunyavirus and Orthomyxovirus perform a prime-and-realign mechanism during RNA 99 synthesis initiation allowing for the addition of terminal repeats at the end of the 100 genome if its correct length is compromised (9) (24) (Fig. 1). Arenaviruses even 101 incorporate a non-templated G in the 5 end of their genomes, a prime-and-realign 102 associated phenomena. However, other viral RdRps follow different strategies for 103 maintaining genome integrity. Particularly, TNTase activity has been reported as a 104 common behavior of viral RdRps. For example, Wuhan nodavirus (WhNV) TNTase 105 activity repairs the 3 initiation site restoring replication initiation in vitro, as a protection 106 mechanism of the 3 ́ template vRNA against cellular exonucleases (25). Among others 107 viral RdRps with TNTase activity we find Sapovirus 3Dpol which has CTP-preference 108 incorporation (26); Hepatitis C virus (HCV) with UTP preferential incorporation (27) or 109 Nodovirus 3Dpol (28) with broader TNTase activity. Besides, TNTase studies of flavivirus 110 HCV and bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) RdRps revealed that changes in template 111 sequences and/or structure could affect the efficiency and preference of nucleotide 112 incorporation (29). To our knowledge, no TNTase enzymatic activity has been reported 113 for Bunyaviricetes L proteins yet. 114 5 115 Figure 1. Scheme of the prime-and-realign RNA synthesis initiation characteristic of 116 bunyaviruses and orthomyxoviruses. The HTNV genome sequence is used. The 117 polymerase starts the RNA synthesis in the second triplet of the genome for de novo 118 initiation of genome replication. After the synthesis of three nucleotides the RNA is 119 realigned upstream for subsequently proceed with the RNA synthesis elongation. 120 121 In this work, we characterize the enzymatic activities of the L protein of HTNV virus as 122 the EN and RdRp activities, and reveal the existence of a TNTase activity. We study the 123 nucleotide and substrate specificity of incorporation. In addition, we extend this finding 124 to other two L proteins from the Bunyaviracetes class: (i) La Crosse virus (LACV) L that 125 belongs to the Elliovirales order and the Peribunyaviridae family and (ii) Crimean Congo 126 Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV) L that belongs to the Hareavirales order and the 127 Nairoviridae family. This finding is relevant for understanding the in vitro activity of 128 these enzymes and the proper interpretation of biochemical assays on bunyaviral L 129 proteins. In addition, by EN assays performed in parallel with the three L proteins we 130 confirm the HTNV and LACV (His+) L proteins as active and the CCHFV (His-) as inactive. 131 Our results have implications for the understanding of L protein’s molecular 132 mechanisms of replication and possible interactions with host RNAs. 133 134 6 Methods 135 136 Expression and purification of L proteins. 137 Codon-optimized gene coding for HTNV L (GenBank reference: NC_005222.1, UniProtKB 138 reference: P23456) and CCHFV L (GenBank ref: NC_005301.3, Uniprot ref: Q6TQR6) 139 carrying N-terminal His-tag followed by TEV protease cleavage site (MGHHHHHH6xHis- 140 tagDYDIPTTENLYFQTEVG) were cloned into pFastBacTM1 donor plasmids. Codon- 141 optimized gene coding for LACV strain LACV/mosquito/1978 L protein sequence 142 (GenBank code: EF485038.1, UniProt code: A5HC98) was cloned without a tag in 143 pFastBacTM1. The HTNV L cap-snatching EN domain (D97A) and RdRp active site (HTNV 144 LSDD1097AAA) mutants were generated by Quick-change site-directed mutagenesis. All 145 recombinant baculoviruses were produced using DH10BACY E. coli competent cells and 146 recombinant proteins were expressed in Trichoplusia ni High 5 cells (Invitrogen PN/51- 147 4005 lot 1783124). For HTNV L, infected cells were harvested at 96 h post-infection by 148 centrifugation (10 min, 4 °C, 5000xg). Following resuspension in buffer A (30 mM Tris- 149 HCl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 2mM TCEP) supplemented with 10 mM imidazole, 150 protease inhibitor cocktail tablets (Roche), MgSO4, DNAase I and RNAse A, cells were 151 disrupted by sonication on ice and centrifuged at 21.000xg for 45 min at 6°C. The 152 clarified supernatant was directly loaded into a Ni-NTA affinity column (HisTrapTM FF 153 crude, GE Healthcare) and washed with buffer A supplemented with 40 mM imidazole. 154 HTNV L was subsequently eluted with buffer A supplemented with 250 mM imidazole. 155 HTNV L fractions were pooled and imidazole concentration was diluted by 2 using buffer 156 A before loading on heparin column (GE, HiTrapTM Heparin HP). Washing step in 9% 157 buffer B containing 30 mM TRIS-HCl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 2 mM TCEP, 1M 158 NaCl was followed by an elution with 30 % of buffer B. HTNV L fractions were 159 concentrated (30-kDa-cutoff Amicon Ultra unit) and further purified by size exclusion 160 chromatography (GE, Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL) with buffer C (30 mM Tris-HCl pH 161 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 5 mM TCEP). Peak fractions analyzed by SDS-PAGE 6% 162 were concentrated and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80 °C for further 163 biochemistry studies. 164 165 7 Untagged LACV L protein was produced as described for HTNV-L protein. High 5 166 infected-cell pellets were resuspended in buffer A (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 167 5 mM beta-mercaptoethanol (BME) and purified by sequential ammonium sulfate 168 precipitation, isocratic gradient elution in heparin column with buffer B (50 mM Tris-HCl 169 pH 8.0, 250 mM NaCl, 5 mM BME) supplemented with 1M NaCl and SEC (Superose 6 170 increase 10/300). CCHFV L polymerase was purified following the same conditions as the HTNV L 173 recombinant proteins. 174 175 Pure proteins analyzed by SDS/PAGE 6% were processed by mass spectrometry facility 176 of Marseille Proteomics (MaP-CRCM). Briefly, gel bands were cut, destained in 100 mM 177 NH4HCO3 in 50% acetonitrile, dried at room temperature, then rehydrated. Cysteines 178 were then reduced using 10 mM DTT in 100 mM NH4HCO3 pH 8.0 for 45 min at 56°C 179 before alkylation in the presence of 55 mM iodoacetamide in 100 mM ammonium 180 bicarbonate pH 8.0 for 30 min at room temperature in the dark, and bands were finally 181 washed twice with 25 mM NH4HCO3 pH 8.0 and digested with high-sequencing-grade 182 trypsin (Promega, Madison, WI). TOSV EN was used as a positive control in all experiments with a buffer 196 8 containing 35 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl and 2 mM TCEP in presence of 2 mM 197 Mn2+ and 0.5 mM DPBA where indicated. After an initial screening performed at 30 °C 198 for 30 min, 1, 3 and 6 h, further experiments were performed at 30 °C for 1h. The 199 reactions were stopped by loading buffer addition (Tris–borate–EDTA, 8 M urea, 5% 200 glycerol). The reaction was also supplemented with 213 5 mM Mg2+ and 0.6 U μl-1 RNAase inhibitor. TNTase reaction was started by adding to 214 the mix 0.2 μCi/μl of the indicated [32P-NTP] and 0.04 mM of the same cold NTP. When 215 in vitro RNA synthesis was studied, reactions were started by adding 0.5 mM 216 GTP/CTP/ATP, 0.04 mM UTP, and 0.2 μCi/μl [32P-UTP]. The resulting mixes were 217 incubated at 30 °C for 3 h. All reactions were stopped by adding 2x loading buffer, 218 heating 10 min at 70 °C and were resolved on a 20% TBE polyacrylamide gels-7 M Urea. 219 The RNA products were separated with 1x TBE buffer for 2h30min. The gels were 220 exposed on a storage phosphor screen and developed with an Amersham Typhoon 221 scanner. 222 All synthetic RNA oligos used for activity experiments were chemically synthesized by 223 Microsynth AG. RNA oligos smaller than 9 nucleotides were acquired from GE Healthcare 224 Dharmacon. In vitro RNA synthesis was studied by radiolabeled [-32P] NTP 225 incorporation in RNA product. analysis.background: Bunyaviricetes viruses cause severe hemorrhagic fever; Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a life‑threatening rodent‑borne bunyavirus that can lead to Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
analysis.methods: In vitro assays of the L protein (RdRp) from HTNV, La Crosse virus (LACV), and Crimean‑Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) were performed to test terminal nucleotidyl transferase (TNTase) activity on double‑stranded RNA substrates and to compare substrate and nucleotide specificity.
analysis.results: HTNV L protein exhibits TNTase activity on dsRNA; other bunyaviral L proteins also display TNTase activity, with differences in substrate and nucleotide specificity across virus families.
analysis.contribution: Shows TNTase as a conserved feature of Bunyaviruses, offering a straightforward biochemical assay for screening RdRp inhibitors and suggesting roles in genome integrity, immune evasion, and RNA metabolism.

papers.title: Multi-omics Reveals Divergent Endothelial Molecular Responses to New and Old World Hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes that vary in clinical manifestation and severity. Although tissue tropism contributes to these differences, both Old and New World hantaviruses infect endothelial cells, where species-specific disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Here we integrated time-resolved global RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics of human endothelial cells infected with New World Andes virus (ANDV) or Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV). Despite equivalent early viral RNA and protein levels, ANDV elicited a stronger innate immune protein response, preceding its restriction while HTNV replication continued. At later stages of infection, HTNV induced downregulation of cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation, accompanied by visual disruption of cellular actin architecture. Additionally, ANDV induced heightened activity of ERBB-family kinases, whose chemical inhibition by neratinib and afatinib reduced viral replication. Together, these data define species-specific responses in endothelial cells, identify druggable host targets, and reveal mechanisms with relevance to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.

​chemical​​inhibition​​by​​neratinib​​and​​afatinib​​reduced​​viral​​replication.​​Together,​​these​​data​​define​ ​species-specific​ ​responses​ ​in​ ​endothelial​ ​cells,​ ​identify​ ​druggable​ ​host​ ​targets,​ ​and​ ​reveal​ ​mechanisms with relevance to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.​ ​INTRODUCTION​ ​Hantaviruses​ ​are​ ​relatively​ ​uncommon​ ​globally,​ ​yet​​infections​​caused​​by​​certain​​species​​can​ ​result​ ​in​ ​severe​ ​disease​ ​with​ ​exceptionally​ ​high​ ​case-fatality​ ​rates.​ ​In​ ​humans,​ ​pathogenic​ ​hantaviruses​ ​cause​ ​two​ ​major​ ​vascular​ ​leakage​ ​syndromes:​ ​hemorrhagic​ ​fever​ ​with​ ​renal​ ​syndrome​​(HFRS),​​classically​​associated​​with​​Old​​World​​hantaviruses​​such​​as​​Hantaan​​virus​ ​(HTNV),​ ​and​ ​hantavirus​ ​cardiopulmonary​ ​syndrome​ ​(HCPS),​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​New​ ​World​ ​hantaviruses​​such​​as​​Andes​​virus​​(ANDV)​​and​​Sin​​Nombre​​virus​​(SNV)​​1,2​​.​​ANDV​​infection​​has​​a​ ​reported​ ​case​ ​fatality​ ​rate​ ​of​ ​~30-40%,​ ​whereas​ ​HTNV​ ​is​ ​~5-15%​​2​,​3​​.​ ​Hantaviruses​ ​are​ ​traditionally​​known​​to​​be​​zoonotic​​viruses,​​maintained​​primarily​​in​​small​​mammal​​reservoirs​​and​ ​transmitted​ ​to​ ​humans​ ​most​ ​commonly​ ​through​​exposure​​to​​excreta​​from​​infected​​rodents​​1,2​​.​ ​However,​​ANDV​​is​​unique​​among​​hantaviruses,​​since​​human-to-human​​transmission​​has​​been​ ​documented​​4,5​​.​ ​Although​ ​ANDV​ ​and​ ​HTNV​ ​share​ ​substantial​ ​genomic​ ​similarity,​ ​the​ ​mechanisms underlying their distinct clinical manifestations remain poorly understood.​ ​laboratory-confirmed​​as​​the​​New​​World​​hantavirus,​​ANDV,​​and​​three​​deaths.​​Despite​ ​ABSTRACT​ ​Hantaviruses​​cause​​vascular​​leakage​​syndromes​​that​​vary​​in​​clinical​​manifestation​​and​​severity.​ ​Although​​tissue​​tropism​​contributes​​to​​these​​differences,​​both​​Old​​and​​New​​World​​hantaviruses​ ​infect​​endothelial​​cells,​​where​​species-specific​​disease​​phenotypes​​remain​​poorly​​understood.​ ​Here​​we​​integrated​​time-resolved​​global​​RNA​​sequencing,​​mass​​spectrometry​​proteomics,​​and​ ​phosphoproteomics​​of​​human​​endothelial​​cells​​infected​​with​​New​​World​​Andes​​virus​​(ANDV)​​or​ ​Old​​World​​Hantaan​​virus​​(HTNV).​​Despite​​equivalent​​early​​viral​​RNA​​and​​protein​​levels,​​ANDV​ ​elicited​ ​a​ ​stronger​ ​innate​ ​immune​ ​protein​ ​response,​ ​preceding​ ​its​ ​restriction​ ​while​ ​HTNV​ ​replication​​continued.​​At​​later​​stages​​of​​infection,​​HTNV​​induced​​downregulation​​of​​cytoskeletal​ ​and​ ​junctional​ ​protein​ ​phosphorylation,​ ​accompanied​ ​by​ ​visual​ ​disruption​ ​of​ ​cellular​ ​actin​ ​architecture.​ ​Additionally,​ ​ANDV​ ​induced​ ​heightened​ ​activity​ ​of​ ​ERBB-family​ ​kinases,​ ​whose​ ​chemical​​inhibition​​by​​neratinib​​and​​afatinib​​reduced​​viral​​replication.​​Together,​​these​​data​​define​ ​species-specific​ ​responses​ ​in​ ​endothelial​ ​cells,​ ​identify​ ​druggable​ ​host​ ​targets,​ ​and​ ​reveal​ ​mechanisms with relevance to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.​ ​INTRODUCTION​ ​Hantaviruses​ ​are​ ​relatively​ ​uncommon​ ​globally,​ ​yet​​infections​​caused​​by​​certain​​species​​can​ ​result​ ​in​ ​severe​ ​disease​ ​with​ ​exceptionally​ ​high​ ​case-fatality​ ​rates.​ ​In​ ​humans,​ ​pathogenic​ ​hantaviruses​ ​cause​ ​two​ ​major​ ​vascular​ ​leakage​ ​syndromes:​ ​hemorrhagic​ ​fever​ ​with​ ​renal​ ​syndrome​​(HFRS),​​classically​​associated​​with​​Old​​World​​hantaviruses​​such​​as​​Hantaan​​virus​ ​(HTNV),​ ​and​ ​hantavirus​ ​cardiopulmonary​ ​syndrome​ ​(HCPS),​ ​associated​ ​with​ ​New​ ​World​ ​hantaviruses​​such​​as​​Andes​​virus​​(ANDV)​​and​​Sin​​Nombre​​virus​​(SNV)​​1,2​​.​​ANDV​​infection​​has​​a​ ​reported​ ​case​ ​fatality​ ​rate​ ​of​ ​~30-40%,​ ​whereas​ ​HTNV​ ​is​ ​~5-15%​​2​,​3​​.​ ​Hantaviruses​ ​are​ ​traditionally​​known​​to​​be​​zoonotic​​viruses,​​maintained​​primarily​​in​​small​​mammal​​reservoirs​​and​ ​transmitted​ ​to​ ​humans​ ​most​ ​commonly​ ​through​​exposure​​to​​excreta​​from​​infected​​rodents​​1,2​​.​ ​However,​​ANDV​​is​​unique​​among​​hantaviruses,​​since​​human-to-human​​transmission​​has​​been​ ​documented​​4,5​​.​ ​Although​ ​ANDV​ ​and​ ​HTNV​ ​share​ ​substantial​ ​genomic​ ​similarity,​ ​the​ ​mechanisms underlying their distinct clinical manifestations remain poorly understood.​ ​Hantaviruses​​have​​recently​​re-emerged​​as​​a​​prominent​​global​​health​​concern.​​In​​2025,​​HCPS​ ​caused​​the​​death​​of​​Betsy​​Arakawa​​in​​New​​Mexico,​​the​​wife​​of​​renowned​​actor​​Gene​​Hackman,​ ​and​ ​three​ ​other​ ​deaths​ ​in​ ​California​​6,7​​.​ ​More​ ​recently,​ ​on​ ​May​ ​2,​ ​2026,​ ​the​ ​World​ ​Health​ ​Organization​ ​(WHO)​ ​was​ ​notified​ ​of​ ​a​ ​cluster​ ​of​ ​severe​ ​respiratory​​illnesses​​aboard​​the​​MV​ ​Hondius​ ​cruise​ ​ship,​ ​which​ ​was​ ​carrying​ ​147​ ​passengers​ ​and​ ​crew​ ​from​ ​23​ ​countries​ ​on​ ​a​ ​voyage​ ​originating​ ​in​ ​Argentina​​6​​.​ ​The​ ​outbreak​ ​resulted​ ​in​ ​13​ ​confirmed​ ​or​ ​probable​ ​cases,​ ​several​ ​laboratory-confirmed​​as​​the​​New​​World​​hantavirus,​​ANDV,​​and​​three​​deaths.​​Despite​ ​research​​efforts,​​no​​effective​​prophylactic​​or​​therapeutic​​direct-acting​​or​​host-directed​​antiviral​ ​agents​ ​have​ ​been​ ​approved​ ​for​ ​hantaviruses​ ​in​ ​the​ ​United​ ​States,​ ​limiting​ ​the​ ​capacity​ ​to​ ​prevent or respond to lethal outbreaks.​ ​HTNV​​and​​ANDV​​cause​​distinct​​clinical​​syndromes​​1,7,8​​that​​differ​​in​​severity​​9–13​​.​​ANDV​​causes​​an​ ​especially​ ​severe​ ​pulmonary​ ​vascular​ ​leak​ ​syndrome​ ​characterized​ ​by​ ​rapid​ ​onset​ ​edema,​ ​hypoxemia,​ ​respiratory​ ​failure,​ ​and​ ​shock,​ ​contributing​ ​to​​its​​high​​case-fatality​​rate.​​Although​ ​both​ ​Old​ ​and​ ​New​ ​World​ ​hantaviruses​ ​have​ ​been​ ​shown​ ​to​ ​efficiently​ ​infect​ ​endothelial​ ​manifestations.​​For​​instance,​​HTNV​​can​​infect​​renal​​endothelial,​​epithelial,​​and​​glomerular​​cell​ ​populations​​1,2​​,​ ​whereas​ ​ANDV​ ​shows​ ​tropism​ ​for​ ​pulmonary​ ​and​ papers.title: AI-generated medical realism and hantavirus misinformation: a new public health threat?
papers.abstract: The widespread availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has substantially reshaped the health-information environment compared with the COVID-19 pandemic. Contemporary AI tools can rapidly generate highly realistic medical-looking content from text, including laboratory reports, radiological images, histological slides, and institutional clinical documentation. During infectious disease outbreaks, such simulated medical content may exploit the visual authority traditionally associated with healthcare institutions and influence public risk perception. During media coverage of the May 2026 Andes virus (ANDV) alert in Italy, news outlets published realistic AI-generated medical imagery depicting hantavirus diagnostic reports, hospital-associated laboratory materials, and outbreak-response scenes linked to real healthcare institutions. One image, in particular, reproduced the visual identity of a real laboratory report produced at "Luigi Sacco" University Hospital despite displaying multiple inconsistencies. In some additional examples, AI generation was not clearly disclosed despite the use of recognizable institutional names and logos. This phenomenon has the potential to extend beyond isolated misinformation events. Emerging evidence indicates that experts may struggle to reliably distinguish AI-generated biomedical and radiological images from authentic materials, raising concern that future infectious disease outbreaks may occur within an information ecosystem increasingly shaped by visually persuasive synthetic media. Such content may amplify public anxiety, distort perceptions of authority, and erode trust in institutions. Synthetic medical realism should therefore be considered a potential emerging category of public-health risk during infectious disease emergencies that requires coordinated action from institutions and regulators developing verification systems, while news media, platforms, and publishers implement AI-disclosure standards and guidelines for synthetic biomedical content.
